title: Char Siu
subtitle: Cantonese barbecue pork with a sticky red glaze
excerpt: Char siu (叉燒) is Cantonese barbecue pork: pork belly or shoulder marinated in hoisin sauce, soy sauce, honey, five spice, and fermented tofu, then roasted until the edges caramelise into a lacquered red crust. It is eaten with rice, used in bao, or served over noodle soup.
sourceNotes: Char siu (literally 'fork-roasted') is one of the most recognized dishes in Cantonese cuisine. Pork strips were traditionally skewered on long forks and held in the opening of a wood-fired oven. The red colour comes from fermented red tofu or red food colouring; in this home version, hoisin and honey are relied upon for the glaze.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cooked char siu freezes well. Slice before freezing. Defrost in the fridge overnight.
recipe.batchNotes: This recipe scales directly. Make a large batch and freeze in portions.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Marinate for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight. The longer the marinade, the better the flavour.

content.text: Pork belly gives the richest result because the fat bastes the meat as it cooks. Shoulder is leaner and produces a more traditional, slightly drier char siu. The key is a long marinade and roasting at high heat so the sugary glaze caramelises rather than just baking through. Baste every 10 minutes during roasting.

items.prepNote: plus 1 tbsp extra for final glaze

content.text: Mix together all the marinade ingredients. Add the pork strips and turn to coat thoroughly. Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight.
Heat the oven to 200°C fan. Place a wire rack over a roasting tin filled with 2 cm of water (the water prevents the drips burning on the tin). Lay the pork strips on the rack, reserving the marinade.

Roast for 15 minutes. Baste with the reserved marinade. Roast for another 15 minutes. Baste again. In the final 5 to 10 minutes, brush with the extra honey and return to the oven: the glaze should be dark, sticky, and beginning to caramelise at the edges.
Rest for 10 minutes before slicing. Char siu is sliced on an angle into 1 cm pieces. Serve over rice with the cooking juices spooned over.

items.symptom: Glaze burns black before the pork is cooked through
items.cause: Oven too hot or not enough water in the tin below
items.fix: Reduce the oven to 180°C and cover loosely with foil. Finish the glaze under the grill at the very end for a final 2 minutes.

content.text: Char siu is eaten on its own with rice, stuffed into bao (barbecue pork buns), sliced over wonton noodle soup, or used in fried rice. A cold leftover char siu sandwich on white bread with hoisin sauce is a worthwhile meal in its own right.
